messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 72
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Refugee Aid Worker
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 53

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened, Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At 72, Minh Tran came to treatment after months of insisting to his wife that he was simply “being careful.” He was a Vietnamese American man who had spent years in refugee aid work, the kind of person colleagues described as steady in a crisis and gentle with frightened families. The event that now occupied him had happened during a field visit connected to his work, when he was traveling with other aid staff to meet newly displaced civilians after a terrorist attack in the region. Their vehicle had slowed near a crowded checkpoint when an explosion tore through the area ahead of them. Minh remembered the blast first as light and force before anything made sense: a violent flash, shattered glass, people dropping, smoke swallowing the road. What stayed with him were fragments rather than a smooth story—images of a body crumpled beside a barrier, a child’s shoe in the dust, the windshield starred with cracks—and, just as sharply, sound. In his mind he still heard the concussive boom, then screaming, then the metallic clatter and shriek that followed as vehicles stopped and people scrambled.

In the days after, Minh told himself he should have done something different. He repeatedly returned to the same thoughts: he should have noticed something suspicious on the road, should have insisted they take another route, should have reacted faster. Even when others reminded him that the bombing had been sudden and indiscriminate, he blamed himself for what happened. He went over the sequence again and again, searching for the moment where, in his mind, he had failed. Yet when he tried to describe the event aloud, he would sometimes stop and look confused, as if he were recounting something that belonged to someone else. The memory felt so extreme that it was hard for him to believe it had happened to him, Minh, a man in his seventies who had spent a lifetime helping others survive upheaval. He could recount certain details vividly, but the whole thing still had an unreal quality, as though it were a scene from a film that had somehow attached itself to his life.

After he returned home, he found that ordinary sounds could make his body react before he had time to think. A dropped pan in the kitchen, a motorcycle backfiring outside, a stack of files hitting the floor at the resettlement office would make him jump hard in his chair. He became constantly watchful, scanning entrances, windows, and the faces of strangers in any public place. He no longer felt broadly safe in the world. Safety shrank to a few tightly defined places—his own bedroom, one corner of the living room, a small office with the door closed. Outside those limited spaces he felt exposed, as if danger could break in without warning.

The road itself became especially difficult. Because the bombing had happened while he was traveling in a vehicle, driving now felt intolerable. At first he avoided the route to work and asked his wife to drive if an errand could not be postponed. Soon he stopped driving altogether, and even riding as a passenger made him tense and silent, his eyes fixed outside, his shoulders rigid whenever the car slowed near intersections or crowded areas. This created immediate consequences for his work. As a refugee aid worker, much of his job had involved meeting clients at community sites, accompanying families between offices, and visiting partner organizations. He started turning down field responsibilities and staying back with paperwork whenever possible. Colleagues noticed that he was no longer willing to travel across town to intake centers. Minh explained it as age, traffic, or fatigue, but privately he knew the problem was the car itself and what the road now represented.

He also began avoiding disagreement in ways that were uncharacteristic. Before, he had been able to advocate firmly for clients when agencies delayed services or when meetings became tense. Now any situation that might involve conflict felt dangerous. If a coworker challenged a plan, he backed down quickly. If a client became frustrated or raised their voice, he would try to leave the room or defer to someone else. At home, he avoided even minor marital disagreements, falling quiet rather than risk confrontation. To Minh, this made sense: conflict no longer felt like a normal part of life but like the beginning of something that could suddenly escalate beyond control.

By the time he sought help, these patterns had narrowed his life considerably. His wife had become his main driver. His work world had contracted to the few spaces where he still felt safe. He remained haunted by visual snapshots of the bombing and by sounds that replayed in his head with disturbing clarity. What finally brought him in was the realization that he had begun declining even meaningful parts of his job, work that had long given him purpose. He said he was afraid that if he kept living this way, his world would become smaller still. At the same time, he hoped for something simple and profound: to sit in a car without bracing for catastrophe, to hear a sudden noise without feeling his whole body jolt, and to believe again that the event belonged to his past rather than waiting for him in every road, every sound, and every moment of tension.
